DEATH OF THE EMPRESS OF RPSSIA 1 The Empress of Russia died at St. Petershurgh on Thursday morning. The deceased Empress, whose life had long been despaired of, and whose recent vt to Cannes in the south of France, was brought to a somewhat abrupt termination in consequence of the manifestation of alarming symptoms, was the only daughter of the late tirmal Duke o, Deese, and sister of his successor, whose son in 1962 married the late Princess Alice of England. She wan horn on the nth td Almost, 1824, and was, tlnrefore, in her Mlth year. Iler Imperial Majesty, who was the And of the late Princess Alice and mother..in-law of the Duke of Edinburgh, visited England on the occasion of the birth of the Duchess of Edinburgh's first child in 18T4, ammpanied by the Cairewitch, and remained the guest of the Queen for some tone.

BONBA T, Tuesday night.—ln reply ton,, address from the Corporation at Bombay, the Viceroy mid : "I have ob- served with great satisfaction the asstrances you give of your loyalty and devotion to the Quesn the Empress of India. It is due, indeed, to the 800 al hely, who has airway. taken a very deep interest in all that concerns t!e welfare of her Indian subjects. ten, deeply sensible of the great res- ponsibility which devolve. upon me in respect of the great office with which Her Majesty has been pleased to entrust me. We are told it does not besome him who putteth on hi. armour to boast himself aa the man who takes it off ; and therefore I are not at all inclined upon this occasion to make to you, end through you to the community of India, any large promises. or to lay before you an extensive pro- gramme. I will only oar this my constant endeavour will be to devote earnestly and assiduously any powers I may possess faithfully to discharge my duty to my Sovereign and to the people of India. Pant famines will prove to have been useful as teaching no to alleviate future nrieery." In respect to the war in Afghanistan the noble Marquis said : No one can think of that contest without feeling his heart beat quicker with honourable and just pride at the recollection of the gallant deed, which in this war, as on so many previous occasions, have been performed for our Queen, our Empress, and our country by Her Majesty's troop., European and native alike ; and we are proud to recollect that in these later times both them err- vices have shown themselves fully able to maintain the great and glorious repntation which the armies of England have won, which the soldiers of England have won for her in every quarter of the globe. But, gentlemen, it will he my mord earnest endeavour to bring that war, so for colic, in my province, tone early and honourable conclusion, in the hope that with returning peace the Government of India may again be able to devote its attention to those works of internal improvement to which you rightly alluded. I can assure you if my lot during my tenure of office may be to contribute in coy degree to the development of the resources of this great country, agriculturally and industrially, and to promote to any extent the happiness and welfare of the people of India, of all ram, creeds, and dames, and PllpeCi- ally to increase the prosperity of the masa of the people, I shall esteem it the greatest honour in my political life."

div.head: TEMPERANCE IEMONSTRATION AT !CORLEY. MR. LEACH. OF ST. HELENS, ON THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION.
div.p: TEMPERANCE IEMONSTRATION AT !CORLEY. MR. LEACH. OF ST. HELENS, ON THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION.

. On Tuesday last, the annual fedire . l omn.ct,n w.th the Norley Indedendent Order of Rechabites was celebrated under very auspous circumstances. The little which may he eited as one of the most remarkable in con- necnon with the temperance movement—wee quite rale, for the occasion,anel much animation wredisplayed in the street where the new Temperance Hall is eituated. About OTc o'clock the members of the order, in the number of about 400, formed a procresion, and, headel tre :he Kingedey Brass Band and the Davenham Drum and Flfe Band, roceedAl through the villreeto Kingsley, where a turn was made. and the proceesiouists visited Morley Hall, the seat of Samuel Woodhouse, Erg, where the grounds and gardens wore generouely thrown open for inspection. The residence of , Mr. Pickering WAS next also the mat of the lion. Arthur Lrerelles. The procresionists afterwanle wended their way back tort, Temperance Hall, where a special tea ' was served. of which about 000 partook. After tea a public mreting Wee held. and the attendance was very large. Mr , J. B Leach, of St. Helen, occuphd the chair, and he WAS eupported by Messrs. J. Dimond. GDR.. of Souttmwt, W. It. Snare, of Liverpool, Bamford, Dutton, and Wright. The Cameras:, in opening the proceedings, said he moat take that opportunity of expressibg to the committee who promoted that organization an I the day's festivities Ids thanks for the honour they had done hint in allowing him prreide over that meeting. They knew that for many years he had to some extent assisted And labound in that part of the country in the temperance cause, arid there woe no pLace nearer iti.l dearer to hie heart than Norley. He always looked to Norlew with plereure, and when a spirit of deepair would hare driven him to give up the cause as hopeless he was urged forward by the remenibrance of how firm they stood to the cause at Worley. They were that day rejoicing in the pleasures of another festival, and reviewing the labours of the pad vrer with delight at their success The lad vear's labours had strengthened their josition, Ae he believed Mr. Dimond would tell them. Had their friends throughout the country many years ago only seen how the Rechabile movement would rise and flourish, and had taken up that branch of the movernent, hi, belief wan that the ramifications of temperance would have been more deeply felt throughout the kingdom. The Rechabile movement, it apprered to him, had barn the missing link in the temper- ance reuse. (Hear, hear.) Ever since it renunenced it bad been proving that. At the present time they were in a better position, and could congratulate themselves on the sucrose of their cause. There were in the areendancy that day, bet they were not to that time last year. The drink had been trying to do Re worst, but they had worsted it in the battle. (Chem.) It hart Wed in its desperate attempt to get the rein. of Government in hand this time. (Hear. hear.) They were sorry when • "hung" Parliament took possession ei St. Stephen's, and reine of their opponents said to them "Where are you now? Here ie a brewers' Parliament elected after all your boasting." Well. some of the temperanre people hung down their heads, but he arm glad to eay that he did not, nor did the people of Norley. (Cheers.) Some people began to think that the end had come, and that all their labours had kern in vain, and that the drink traffic was tortweep them out of existence. , His own impression was that • reaction would take place, and the country would open its eves. The country bad now !awakened itreli, hut not before the brewery Parliament had done terrible work, and when it did awake the brewer, tun. pled over like ninepins, end Sir Wilfrid Lawson felt ex- , tremely jolly—as he expressed it—at their downfall. (Cheers) The brewers were a class of people that ought not to sit in the Houte of Commons. (Flear, hear) Ile was afraid they were actuated to • certain extent by personal motive., and in came cases to much so that they could be scarcely trusted to do their duty to their constituents. Ile sat lathe House of Commons one night and heard a brewer make a nix hours' speech with the intention of wearying the House with arguments against the Sunday Closing I:files/ion in Ireland, but he was pleased that Mr. Gladstone bore it with patience and dorms! till six o'clock in the morning to beat the finish of Mr. Murphy's vetch. Since the late re- action the brewers were beginning to may that they were , always friend. with three who elects/ this Parliament, but it WA. nn ure deceiving them in that manner. Thor had rot the brewers down and they meant to keep them down— (hear, hear)—and intended to stmngle them before they had done with them (Cheers.) Recently a big seat in the church was given tea brewer, and the brewers' Parliainent bad made some of their members into baronets. Well, they had got their reward. It wee pleas- ing, however, to notice that the Church were finding that they had committed a fatal blunder in shaking hands with the brewer for the a.ke of his nioney They were cutting *grinder those ties, and the Established I Church was beginning to throw the brewers overboard I (Hear, hear.) But . when we conside- the smolt fee charged, as well as the . lowest charge poasible to all its excursions, cud the know- ledge of natural history certain to be acquired, it inc pity they stied in their own light. Chester Field Club numbere over 500 member, Runcorn should have not lees than 100 members. Doubtless there will be a large accession of memberehip by the next field day, on the 12th June. IVe have been led to these remarks by the excursion on Saturday bit, when the party, which mustered a little over I wenty, left Runcorn at 2-15 pan. for Five Creases. At Frodeham amtion they were joined by Mr. James F. Robinson, who 1.1 them first through the grounds of Mr. E. A. Wright, Pork- place. They were deligheed with the conservatory, noticing the her orange trees in fruit, and the well-grown herb meow calceolaria, and India-rubber plants. They also observed a quantity 01 mistletoe on the apple and near trees in the garden. Afterwards they quietly walked to Five Crosses, where tea woe provided by Mrs. Andrews. Before 'separating, a vote of thanks Noe pro- ' posed and carried unanimously, to Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P , for his courtesy in permitting the party to eee hin gardens, Sy 'Pea being heartily enjoyed, they then leisurely strolled down ?AMC pretty lanes to Bradley. gathering many wild flowers on the way. Reaching the village they went through Jennings Clough, a wild spot, where pelysiichum angulare, conlamine unhurt, lathyrus tuberoses, enchanter's nightshade, and cuckoo pint were picked. The side of the glen in many plate, was white with the wild ramsone and snowball tree, adding much to the beauty of the scene. Coming from the fields they then were privileged to go over to Mr. Dutton's garden, a thoroughly enjoyable epot there the forget-me-not was seen in immense tulle, many feet in length, also fern. in profusion. They left for the station with much reluctance, which, without any accident, and pleased with the charming day they had spent, they reached a lithe after eight o'clock. The prize for the excureion was awarded to Mrs. Summertield, for the best collection of plants belouging to the natural order CaryeThyllaectr, or pink family. Mr. Matthew., of Weston, solved the enigma on the paper, it being upon the fertile. or infertile flower, of the dog violet.

OF CORK'S CHITIATI.—CPLPIMATION AT Or. Mtcusax's, Drcrow—On Sunday Afternoon the feast of Corpus Christi woe celebrated with ninth gorgeotimes of ceremonial at St. Michael's beautiful Roman Catholic Church, Ditton, which was crowded in every part. The alters pre- sented a splendid appearance. having been artistically decorated with evergreens, dower, and hot-house plants. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Father Hasa, who took for his text John XII. 12-13 v. The speaker briefly referred to the entrance of the Saviour into Jerusalem a few days before Hi, osnion, when He was met by the multitude. , bearing palm branch, and said this was the first procession ,in which Jesus took part. A few days later there took place another procession. the Son of Mary being led up to Mount Calvary. Though Jesus was no or ger visible to them in oodily shape, he had remained with them in the Most Blessed Sacrament of the Eucharist, which they carried in procession in the Catholic Church at the Feast of Copper Christi. It was in their power to have Christ himself really present with them on the altar. They might ask wait it not in vain that they bowed down before the monstrance, and to A., that k was Jesus Christ Hiniwlf whom they had heft.; them P No, it was not ia vain. It we, a sacrament, blessed by their Lord nineteen centuries ago and in spite of all which had been said and done against the Catholic Church , it yet stood unmoved in the hearts of 200 million. 0 peotde. • • Jems Christ was present really and substantially. for the ! bread and wine had been changed into the body andl.l,l of Christ. Some of them might ask how it was possible that Christ could be in that small monstrance. Never mind the , possibility. Leave that to God. Let them ask thernielves if God said so. He answered that he did ; and if , Got , could not deceive them: and their procession that day would not onlybeo procession of triumph, hut one of thanksgiving. He advised them to follow the procession with beads un- covered, in silence and prayer. The procession, in which • about 1,511/ persons took part, then formed in the church in the following order :—Behind the first banner, all the boys, girls, and young men, and voting women in the order as appointed. Then followed the members of the church, the the choir, the priests, and the canopy with the Blessed Sacra- ment, behind which the male members of the congregation two by two, followed by the female portion of the congreara. tion, also two by two. In this order the procession paraded the grounds of the college until they arrived before • temporary altar of beautifal deeign, erected on the hall steps, where the ceremony of the elevation of the sacrament ou gone through, and the Litany which was beautifally rendered by the choir of the church, which is composed entirely of German, The proceseim then proceeded to the church, where the Benediction and Litany were gone through, and the nenice terminated.

The minutes of the Sanitary Committee comprised an order for payment of accounts amounting to £OB 19s. 31. It was recommended that tenders be advertised for the pur- chase and weekly removal of the manure made at the Cor- poration stables for the next 12 months; that the Town Clerk again give notice, in pursuance of "The Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milk Shops Order, of July, 1879," of the requirements of the order, and of the mode of registration of all persona aerrying on any of the trades within the meaning of the order ; that the Town Clerk write to the Water Works Corn- puny again requesting them to supply that part of Latchford , beyond Black Bear Bridge with water, and informing them that unless they now consent to do so, application will be made to the Local Government Board by the Corporation for power to supply that district with water ; and that the tender of Messrs Gibson and Son for the alterations to Orel bath rooms at the infections diseases hosp;tal, at £I2I 55.,1 ' be accepted. ICouncillor MONKS, in moving the confirmation of the I minutes, referred to the water supply of Latchford. He said I the cooled.tee felt that the Water Works Company were not acting in a broad and generous spirit to Latchford in withholding a good water supply, and one of the minutes which had been read was an indication of the action the committee would be bound to take if • proper water supply could not he given to Latchford. Water was very essential to health and clbanliness, and no doubt whilst it was the : wish of the company to make a good profit, on the other hand it WNS the wish of the committee that the people should • be well supplied with water. He hoped the Water Works Company might see their way to lay on a eutToient supply lon Latchford, and so avoid any unpleasant action on the part of the Sanitary Committee. Councillor MILNER seconded the passing of the rninnten. Councillor Poo,. said Connoillor Monks hail just I remarked that the Waterworks Company were not acting in a broad and generous stunt with regard to Latchford. He wished to saw that the compeny were not acting in a broad or by any means generous spirit with regard to any part of 11,. town, and complaints were frequent as to the treatment of the public at the hands of the company. The company seemed to be taking every measure to screw out of the town as much aS they could, and public convenience was entirely I lost sight of. Their sole object seemed to be to screw as much as they could nut of the town, and he did not think I ittli7Zl.fra'irei'al'cl"est.heantlthheev'eru,l•eers'i':elZe o7tl7ehpekohplie',Ut'odull ;he in the hands of a private water company. The Conceit, would he compel let some time to take the supply into their ' ' own hands, and the sooner the better. He thought the Waterworks were entirely In the wrong hands at the present time, and the powers they possowed were being used—how., going to say in an unscrupulous manner—but at all events he would say in an ungenerous manner. Councillor Kusw thought some crblit was due to the ! Waterworks Company. They had been labouring for along ! time under difiiculties, and no doubt there was a time when they had no return for their outlay. They took steps to get additlonal water from Winwick, and hews, told that there was now an unbounded supply. He should be surprised to hear they were not anxious to supply Latchford with water. He hoped the committee would do all they could to prevent the necessity of appealing to the Local Government Board. He was en ry to hear Councillor Platt's remarks, but he thought if the company were fairly approached they would be inclincd Co give way on many matters now complained, of.

Councillor C 610.11,.. said the Sanitary Committee were informed by the company that they must guarantee them a certain income before they laid down the pipes. The Rev. dons 10060 rote to call the attention of the Board ton matter which he thought justly claimed a little ounsideration. He supposcal it was a matter of fact—at j ' present he was to infortned—that the presence of gentlemen 1. of the Press at their Board meetings, was a matter of prnvi- ' lege and not of right, and that they were there by permiseion of the Board to make such notes and commence npon what passed as seemed proper and desirable. Ile apprehended there were non, of ithem who would wish to exclude the gentlemen of the Pre., particuLarly those who represeutol the local newspapers--the Warrington pope.. But it tease question, it his mind, as to whether it was altogether desir- able that they shonld have representatives of the Press from Liverpool or Mancbeeter present at theirdeliberations-1 bear hear,)—and certainly it was undesirable that any gentle- man who represents the Press in those cities, ehould con- struct sensational paragraphs which were simple extracts of what took piece inn tine deliberations of that Board. Ile remembered 'idling there in his place. and, having come , actors Chat tine, bill, lie asked, without rising from his seat, the meaning of it, perfectly oblivious of the fact that gentlt. men of the Press were peewee. But presently he (maid Iffincelf advertised all over Liverpool in the Liverpool Echo on having asked some questions. On the previous night a paragraph appeared which had excited the iiiterest of the members of the Board, at he saw several gentle:nen had provided themselves with copies of the paper. lie called attention to that paragraph, not because Inc obj,cleol b, any fair criticism on any conduct which might ohoae- teri. them there, but because he could not help thioking they hnta been very largely misrepresented in what had taken place. (Hear, hear.) Of comae, they all knew that newspaper reporters had • strong temptation to construct racy p dagraphs, as the public were on the look-out for anitething sensational ; but lie thopght it was only fair to the Board that the truth should be stated, and nothing but , the truth. They were told they hail gained an unenviable notoriety, which he thought might be somewhat true, but Its thought it was a matter for doubt as to whether the Board showed "great collective inability." They might have been guilty, some of them, of making use of expres- sions in their speechna which were not altogether elegant, but be did not think they showed much inability. More- over, the public were told that disputes were of frequent occurrence, and that frequently the Board were in the habit of having recouree to the Local liovernment Board to settle their diaput.. That, he undertook to say, was net true. Since he bad been • member of the Board, that wae for two years, there had not t.en one. The article went on 10 say that inquiries had been hold on almost every conceivable subject." He did not know that the Board had had a very fare number of inquiries, but, as to the inquiry which wan now asked for, he did not think it arose from any want of power on their part to settle matters, but because they would , rather the tiovernment authorities should tell them where the fault lay with regard to the removal question. He could , not help thinking that disputes and diecussions bad Aileen, not from any irritability on the part of the Baaril, hut from the emlottered state of the sfficials. He callol attention to , the matter, nut from any wish to exclude .y gentleman conning there, but to seggest tni the gentlemen of the l'ress , the propriAy of being fair to tne Board and to the public. , (Hear, hem.) Major CARTWRIGHT said he did not complain much of what the representatives of the Press wrote or what they said, because he thought he had been about the best abused ; man at the Board through tine l'ress. But what lie bad done he had done in the intoned,, of those who had sent him r there, and he did not .tre what the reporters wro to so long , as he knew he was doing that which was right. (Hear, • hoar.) If he was asked in his .pacity as a Ottani'en to do r anything that entitled him to an &newer, he thought he ought b. have it. If the Chairman ruled that he ought not , to have it he was perfectly rentistiont But he thought as a member of this Board, that when he asked a question upon , any matter connected with that Board and it was a clear and legitimate question, and the Chairman did not rule hint out r of order, he was entitled toil. He had no doubt a grentt , deal of those remarks had arisen through him being determined, as far as he was concerned, to sift into nutters , where he had found there had been any negligence ; and lie was sorry to rind li, it oven tine previous week there was a gtntlenien of the Hoard who said he was making a serious , charge. Now, he did not make any serious charge against anybody, nor was Itemn favour of having a Local finvern- ' ment Board enquiry, becauso hid experience of Local tiovernment Board enquiries—and they had had several of , them—was that they had always ended in etnoke. lie knew of nni Government enquiry that liad ever as it were held : water. In his opinion this matter of going to the Local liovernment Board was a mistake, and ought to be settled by that Board. That was his impression, and as tones ha was concerned he vras very sorry there wan going to be an inquiry, because he knew what the end of it would be. There was no necessity for it atoll. It simply remained for that Bmird to take its proper action to insist upon any orders , of that Board being .rrid out, and to see that they were ! carried out by those who were appointed according to the standing ordern. That was all that was required. Mr. Conran stid the Board ehoull be careful as to how they crippled the representatives of the Press, as their con- stituents had a perfect right to have ooethatinn report of the proceedings of that Board. Mr. !icemen.nr said as Major Cartwright bad thought lit to refer to &remark ,node by him last week that the Major made a serious charge, he thought it was within the memory of every gentleman at that Board that what he (Mr. Black- horst) mid was perfectly true, and he main.ined will that Major Cartwright made a .rioun charge. The Major said tlmt in consequence of the negligence or inattention of some oflieial the ratepayers had lost the sum • of Lei, and if that was not a serioue charge he did not know what was. 11 11,00 charge was true, it wee only just that the Local tiovernment Board should put the blame on the right shoulders. As to the representatives of the Presa, he did not think they used discretion. Ile did not think the ' Board /ghoul,' meet as gentlemen, and that certain represen- tatives should coine to the meetings and report a portion of the business in order to conetruct sen.tionel paragraphs. He did not see why the Board should be held up to ridicule wefk after week any more than other Board, were. •• " . .

Mr. Ilatd. quite agreed with Mr. 1 onge that some discre- tion should be used in what was reported. But there was something more than that If they were going to talk about that matter they were going to advertise themselves still more. Ile did not see why they should complain—he did not we that they had any reason to complain—of the reports of the business traneacted there. It was only the other week the proceedings at a meeting of a Board of Guardians at Manchester equalled anything that had taken place at that Board. Ile did not think the Board ought to cotnplain, and if they let the matter end they would do right, as im thought , the public would judge rightly of what the members of that Board were doing. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Honotnoc said he aympathised very much indeed with the very sensible tiCeervations Mr. Yonge had used with reference to what had appeared in the Li.erpool Echo. From time Co time the Board had been greatly ridiculed, i and charged with diwussing their businese in a discreditable , manner, aud also with gross inability. He agreed with Mr. Yong,. in saying that those charges were, to say the loud, exaggerated. For instance, in reference to the Local Government Board enquiries. There were very few the Board had ever had, but he did not think any one, after cahn deliberation, would say they were not lit to send to the Local Government Board for their opinion. As to the last one—he did not wish to introduce any irrelevant Ire did did think that the resolution to send toll. la:cal Govern- ment Board was a very foolish one. He did think it wasone that Board sh,,uld have settled, and expeseed a firm opinion tipm it—(bear, hear,)—and one which ought not to have presented the slightest difficulty in arriving at a conclusion. He would be the last to exclude representative of the Frew from coining there. Ile would give them the fullest latitude, and, as a tole, there was no doubt they exercised the discre- tion with which they were gifted inn sensible manner. But he dia think there was a little drawing on the imagination in the paragraph referrol to. He thought the Guardia, as a rule, compared very favourably indeed with any Board of Guardia, in the country. Ile could not help, unfottunately,some of the officials cross-questioning, but the Warrington Board of Guardians, as at present constituted, was an immense iniprovement upon the Board that existed there 30 or 40 years ago. (Laughter.) They never heard welt terms an" liars ;" they never heard threata held out of personal chastisement. Why, some 40 years ago, the argu- ment was employed in that way, and culminated in one gentleman threatening to throw an inkstand TI another gentleman's head. (Laughter.) Well, they had nothing of that kind now, and he thought the conduct of the Warring- ton Guardians would very favourably compare with other Boards of Guardians in tho country. He was not at all aeharned of what had been done, hut if a gentleman asked a question he was entitled to have a civil answer. (Hoar, hear.) If they were not asked in a civil manner, well, no doubt, gentlemen were liable to lose a little temper hut he did not think any harsh criticism needed to be passed upon their deliberations. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Wistereat yr said there was not a Guardian who would desire to see the gentlemen of the I Freon excluded from that roora. (Hear, hear.) The more fully they reported the protnedings of the Board the better; but he must object to the incomplete statements that had from time to time appeared. Take that little ques- tion that Mr. Tongs had alluded to. If in the report. that Ita,l been given in various pama, about the salmon, it had been said that the Board of (in:Lelia, oaths 6th of April. 1377, bought Bibs. of fish at 2,. Rd. a pound, he thought the public would not have regarded that as a very extravagant proceeding. They would have come to the conclusion, he was sore, that it was very Ind taste indeed for anybody to throw into the teeth of the Board a matter that had taken plate more than three years ago, and which the me- w,: DORM hld nothing to do with. With reference to what aL. Cooper had said stoat every little thing being re- ported, he thought that would be wrong. It was better, to leave it tm time discretion.of the reporter-ow else the reporters would report some of them verbatim, and the would throw :tones at themselves by eeeing their speeches in print. The enatugaw, referring to the report in the E, to, raid if those remarks had applied to a person in business he should have thought them libellous. He had not the leane ob)ec.ion to the reporters being present, hut be thought that what appeared in print ought te I, strictly true. He did sot see the incompetency of that Board to do its business, and if it was said he war incompetent r conduct his business in • pr. irGnner he should have thought it libellous. The subject was then allowed to drop.

...„ A heave lees hoe been experienced by the Catholic popu- lation of Bt. Helens in the death of the Rev. W. Brindle. who for upwards ot eight year& war attached to Holy Cross Church, and during his min,strations in this part of the diocese earned the goodwill and esteem nt all classes of the community. Naturally of an urbane disposition, he Inv the more successful in gathering anon,! and &Nod him whilst here. very taro circle of fri uds and wpll.wishers. Earnest in his sealoue endea-ours to carry on the religion. duties of the Church with rilpity, yet always encouraging, and by his word. and presence always helping to ameliorate and improve the condition of many of the congregation, and et the same time to prornote a feeling of friendship and love towards each other outside its pale, be gained for himself not only the affection of all be came in contact with, but the re- spect of disinterested persons wlm regarded his labours with anything but feelings of antagmusm. The deceased gentle- man was of a Wigan family, which numbered, we believe, seven stalwart sons, three or four of whom were priests, the two surviving clergymen being the Rev. Father T. Brindle, of Oldham. and the Rev. Ralph Brindle, of Present, and three tiner clergymen. so far as personal appearance and deportment go, bare eeldom sprung from one f.,mily. The late Father Brindle was removed from St. Helens, con- sequent upna changes in the districts of the catholic clergy- men in 1873 tn St. Bueno's College, North Wales where be remained some time when being overmken by ill health he WAS taken to bin brother's It Present, where he remained in suffering for a considerable length of time, during which he submitted to An operation. When c..nrAlescent it was • great comfort to him to see many of his old parishioners and friends who journeyed from St. Helens, and were per. mitred to visit him at intervals, and who nceired

visits in return when he was able to go about. Shortly after this the deceased reverend gentleman removed to St. Prancis Xavier's Clnych. Liverpool, where hi, health agaM failed hint, and he was again necemitat,d to seek rest, and for that Purpose returned to Present. Here he was attended by Dr. Twyford, of St. Helens, but notwithstanding the most as- sidunus attention he continued to grow- worse and died on Sunday morning last. Thu slay la, l,..ing the Feast of Corpus Christi, and a special day servic the c.,ngregation at Holy Cross Church were informed of the illness of the reverend gentleman, and were earnestly exhorted to off, up Prayer, for hire. None, however, were prepared foe the solemn news which greeted them on attending the church on Sunday morning, when his dentin' was announced. To prevent a eurprise that mi:tht bare resulted in proving too great a sh..ck if the new. was ' merely announced from the pulpit. the thoughtful precau- tion had been taken of inf..nniug the members of the con- gregation an they entered the doom fin need scarcely say the announcement was r,.c..ivel with the deepest sorr ho all. At Holy Cross Church, the pl-,ce the deceased was pardonably proud of and loved owe!, h.,1..re the .ermon at the principal maw. the Rev. Father Fgnom, S.J., who spoke with much eniotion, said the hand that hod PO often been lifted op in their behalf in the holy sacrifice of the mass now lay cold in death, and he beer A them to re. member how he had lalnured for them. Tlmugh they were sure he had now gone ta his eternal reward they shonld do all they .uld for him in return by thew pray..rs. At the conclusion of the mem and after the evening service, Mt. trnsworth played the "Dead march. in Saul,- nn the organ. Rees thought that the interment imalit p.ssitily bellowed to lake place in St. Helens, but the rem tins of the dec.atted were interred on Tuesday la.t. :it Ginn... On Tuesday evening.. M. Peter Rylands, se will he seen from our report of Parliamentary 'Proceedings originakst deflate in the House of Commorm on the Government of Cyprus. 'Referring to Mr. Hylands's epeech the Daily Seas save Mr. Rvlands's speech "mermen( reinarkahle ability. an.d gave a complete, and in some passages a very aninsing 'description, of the extraordinary velem which prevailed in Cyprus during the interval of its administration under the "

The London correspondent of the Li rerpoof Dail y Post says: —Mr. Rylands lea humorous and facile speaker upon a great variety of recondite selects. He readies all he mys with the most satisfactory results, marshalling ltis facts with in. geouity, and bringing up little squadrons of quaint jokes aid eccentric lor, which render boo one of the most interesting epeakers in the rank and Its of the faithful Commons. We have all of us pleasant recollections of the admirable speech in which the bon. member for Burnley indicated the financial policy of the late Government acear ago and those r,col- 'echo. whetted the curiosity of hon. members to-day to hear what he hail to say about Cyprus. Mr. Rylands was jfavour," with a very good house. Mr. Gladstone and Mr. • Bright remained in their places, the triton Minister with his head turned towanl the hon. gentleman and his face full of interest. Mr. Ryland, began by asserting that Cyprus as a British possession was the out-come of the drmmy romance of an English novelist who conceived the Angle- Turkish Convention forty years ago, and gave it being as the late Prime Minister. Mn ridiculed the usefulness of the island as a British possession, and twitted the Into Under Seretary for ' Foreign Affairs upon the failure of his prophecim in regard ito the island. He convulsed the House by citing a few staneeeof departmental blundering in connection with the : transfer of Cyprus. One instance, he said, was when a thoreeand hnge coal boxes, each of which required four men to carry it, were sent out to Cyprus, while 3S a matter of fact there was no coal to burn nor a mingle fue.place in the whole island. Another pleasantry of Mr. Rvlands was a statement that i• addition to the coal boxes the la'e Go- vernment sent mit neveral hundrols of warming pans for use by her Majesty's troops in an tßiand where the tempera- ture registered 115 and 120 legrees. He also cited as an instance of the sort 44 personn we employ to collect .r • Cyprian taxes that the collectors decorated their heads with dish covers Ile made a. general attack upon the adminis. tration of the island, declaring that tile adniinistration was unjuet, oppressive, :ind cruel to the Christian sull.cts, and unworthy of the British Empire. Mn. Rylands spoke about j an hour, and delivered a very effective speech in support of , hie motion, and on his conclusion was loudly cheered. I

A correepondent in the Manchester Guardtan writer :a follows :—ln Mr Rylands's motion respecting Cyprus the peers displayed deep interest, and amongst those who frorn time to time came into the gallery over the dock were the Archbishop of York, Earl Beauchamp, Lord Norton. Lord Minmarleigh. Lord Bradhourne, Lmd Aberdare. and Lord Cotteslx. and after the other Rouse had adjourmd there also arrived the Earl of Derby, the Duke of Marl- borough, the Earl of Caraperdown, and Lord Bury. The Liberals collected in force on their side in the body of the House. but the Opposition benches were never more than half filled, and the attendance of Tories soon fell toe lore point. ?dr. Bradlaugh was present under the gallery. Mr. Ryland, treated his theme with force, vigour, and effxt, and in the earlier portion of hi, address subjected the delud- ing representations of the late liovernment, their unfulfilled predictions. and their management of affairs to the severe test of scathing satire. to was his view that we had simply acquired Cyprue in fulfilment of the fanciful schemes of the youthful author of "Tancred," but when he went on to declare that the island was worthies, and had !wen obtained tr diecreditable means, the Torirs. offering a temporary resistance to his onslaught. joined in a chorus of Noes." They were unable. however, to refrain from sharing in the merriment promoted by Mr. Rylands's humorous description of the sapient action of the late tioverument in sending out cargoes of coal boxes to a place where coals and fire-plares were unknown. and providing copper rearming pans for the comfort of troops afflicted with fever under a tropierl sky. The hon. menthe' engszed the close attention of Lis audi• enee for an hour, and the ni.jmity haying meanwhile pre- served their favourite judicial attitude with much strictness, rewarded him with hearty plaudits et the close.
